title: Πλέοντες
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 308 (= Perry 78). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: Certain men, having gone aboard a boat, were sailing.
sentences.n: ἐμβαίνω, 'step in', is the regular verb for going aboard. σκάφος is properly the hull, the hollowed thing, and so stands for the vessel itself.

sentences.t: Γενομένων δὲ αὐτῶν πελαγίων, συνέβη χειμῶνα ἐξαίσιον γενέσθαι καὶ τὴν ναῦν μικροῦ καταδύεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Genomenōn de autōn pelagiōn, synebē cheimōna exaision genesthai kai tēn naun mikrou katadyesthai.
sentences.l: And they having come to be on the open sea, it happened that a monstrous storm arose and that the ship all but went under.
sentences.i: When they were out on the open sea, a monstrous storm came on and the ship all but went under.
sentences.n: πελαγίων is an adjective where English wants a phrase: 'having become of-the-open-sea', that is, out beyond sight of land. μικροῦ is a genitive of measure, 'within a little', and so 'all but'. συνέβη takes accusative and infinitive, 'it came about that'.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ πλεόντων ἕτερος περιρρηξάμενος τοὺς πατρῴους θεοὺς ἐπεκαλεῖτο μετ’ οἰμωγῆς καὶ στεναγμοῦ χαριστήρια ἀποδώσειν ἐπαγγελλόμενος, ἐὰν περισωθῶσι.
sentences.tr: Tōn de pleontōn heteros perirrēxamenos tous patrōious theous epekaleito met’ oimōgēs kai stenagmou charistēria apodōsein epangellomenos, ean perisōthōsi.
sentences.l: And one of those sailing, having torn his clothes about him, called upon the gods of his fathers with wailing and groaning, promising that he would render thank-offerings if they should be brought safely through.
sentences.i: One of those aboard tore his clothes about him and called on the gods of his fathers with wailing and groaning, promising thank-offerings if they should come through safe.
sentences.n: περιρρήγνυμαι in the middle is to tear one's own garment open around oneself — the Greek gesture of grief and of entreaty. οἱ πατρῷοι θεοί are the gods of one's own house and line, the cult a man inherits. χαριστήρια are the offerings vowed in return for a rescue. ἐάν with the subjunctive keeps the very words of the vow.

sentences.t: Παυσαμένου δὲ τοῦ χειμῶνος καὶ πάλιν καινῆς γαληνῆς γενομένης, εἰς εὐωχίαν τραπέντες ὠρχοῦντό τε καὶ ἐσκίρτων, ἅτε δὴ ἐξ ἀπροσδοκήτου διαπεφευγότες κινδύνου.
sentences.tr: Pausamenou de tou cheimōnos kai palin kainēs galēnēs genomenēs, eis euōchian trapentes ōrchounto te kai eskirtōn, hate dē ex aprosdokētou diapepheugotes kindynou.
sentences.l: And the storm having ceased and a fresh calm having come again, having turned to feasting they were dancing and leaping, inasmuch as they had escaped from danger against all expectation.
sentences.i: When the storm had ceased and the calm came back fresh, they fell to feasting and went dancing and leaping about, since they had escaped a danger they had not looked to escape.
sentences.n: ἅτε with a participle gives the reason as a fact the narrator vouches for; ὡς with a participle would give it as the men's own view of the matter. ἐξ ἀπροσδοκήτου is an adverbial phrase, 'out of the unexpected', and goes with the participle. The two imperfects ὠρχοῦντο and ἐσκίρτων hold the revelry open for the helmsman to interrupt.

sentences.t: Καὶ στερρὸς ὁ κυβερνήτης ὑπάρχων ἔφη πρὸς αὐτούς· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ φίλοι, οὕτως ἡμᾶς γεγηθέναι δεῖ ὡς πάλιν, ἐὰν τύχῃ, χειμῶνος γενησομένου. »
sentences.tr: Kai sterros ho kybernētēs hyparchōn ephē pros autous· « All’, ō philoi, houtōs hēmas gegēthenai dei hōs palin, ean tychēi, cheimōnos genēsomenou. »
sentences.l: And the helmsman, being an unbending man, said to them: « But, friends, we must rejoice in such a way as though a storm will come again, if it should so chance. »
sentences.i: And the helmsman, who was a hard man, said to them: « But, my friends, we should take our joy as men who know that another storm may come. »
sentences.n: ὡς with a genitive absolute in the future (χειμῶνος γενησομένου) gives the ground as the speaker's own view of the case: 'on the understanding that a storm will come again'. ἐὰν τύχῃ, 'if it should so chance', is dropped in parenthetically. στερρός is 'stiff, hard' — of a man, unbending. γέγηθα is a perfect with present force, so γεγηθέναι is to be in a state of gladness, not to have become glad.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος διδάσκει μὴ σφόδρα ταῖς εὐτυχίαις ἐπαίρεσθαι τῆς τύχης τὸ εὐμετάβλητον ἐννοουμένους.
sentences.tr: Ho logos didaskei mē sphodra tais eutychiais epairesthai tēs tychēs to eumetablēton ennooumenous.
sentences.l: The story teaches not to be lifted up overmuch by good fortune, bearing in mind the changeableness of chance.
sentences.n: ἐπαίρομαι is to be raised up, and so elated, with the dative of what does the raising. τὸ εὐμετάβλητον is a neuter adjective under the article, Greek's standard way of naming a quality: 'the easily-changed thing', changeableness. ἐννοουμένους is accusative because it agrees with the unexpressed subject of the infinitive.
